newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia aid workers pulled out of Bougainville.
newsitem.headline: Australia aid workers pulled out of Bougainville.

text.p: Australia on Tuesday evacuated its aid workers from strife-torn Bougainville and closed vital medical aid projects on concerns about rising tensions on the Papua New Guinea island wracked by a secessionist rebellion.
Australian Foreign Minster Alexander Downer said the Bougainville situation had led him to abandon a planned visit to Mauritius for the launch of a forum of Indian Ocean rim nations.
"Although I had planned to attend the meeting, it is now necessary for me to remain in Australia because of important issues involving Papua New Guinea," Downer said in a statement.

The Papua New Guinea military on Tuesday denied a rebel charge that mercenaries had launched a mortar attack on the mountainous, jungle-clad South Pacific island, 800 kms (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby.

A spokesperson for the Australian government's aid agency, Ausaid, told Reuters its workers had been pulled out of Bougainville and vital medical projects temporarily closed because of concerns for the workers' safety.
"We did it because of the security situation," she said.
The move affects four aid workers. Plans for another eight to go to Bougainville next month have also been put on hold.

The decision, which leaves the island with only one civilian doctor, followed rebel warnings that foreigners could be in danger because of the government decision to use mercenaries in a bid to end the nine-year insurgency.
The rebels' Bougainville Interim Government on Tuesday said mercenaries had fired three mortar rounds towards the capital, Arawa, in the centre of the island the day before.
But PNG defence force Chief-of-Staff Jack Tuat denied the report. He said Arawa was held by government troops and there were no mercenaries on the island.
"Arawa is regarded as a pacified area and we are looking after the livelihood of the people there. Why would we attack our own town?" Tuat said by telephone from Port Moresby.
But Tuat said a "skirmish" may have occurred outside Arawa between government troops and rebels.
The rebel statement also said mercenary-led government troops had landed on Bougainville and taken up positions near the island's giant Panguna copper mine.
Rebels forced the closure of the mine in 1989. Papua New Guinea on Sunday said it wished to buy back foreign interest in Panguna and reopen it, providing compensation for landowners.
Rebel leader Francis Ona charged that Port Moresby would let the resource-rich island be plundered by foreign miners, with four new mines opened once the island was secured.
Ona told Australian Broadcasting Corporation that renewed mining would destroy the island and scuttle any hopes of peace.
"We truly believe that all the island of Bougainville is under threat of destruction by these foreign companies," said Ona in an interview aired on Tuesday.

Papua New Guinea has hired mercenaries through British-based Sandline International and says they are training its troops for a mission to Bougainville. Australia, New Zealand, Britain, the United States and South Africa have criticised the move.
